# Stripe
Help increase the GDP of the internet.
Technology, Information and Internet • South San Francisco, California • 1,527,345 followers • 5,001-10,000 employees

## Overview
Stripe builds programmable financial services. Millions of companies—from the world’s largest enterprises to the most ambitious startups—use Stripe to accept payments, grow their revenue, and accelerate new business opportunities. Headquartered in San Francisco and Dublin, the company aims to increase the GDP of the internet.

**Stripe** (1d): Conor McNamara sits down with investor and tech analyst Philipp Klöckner to discuss the impact of AI on the global economy, arguing that regions with the most affordable energy and natural resources will win. They explore what the automation wave means for Germany’s labor shortages, and the critical need for a cultural shift, where engineers build new companies that accelerate economic growth: https://lnkd.in/gpbJvvnF . [Likes: 113, Comments: 10]; **Stripe** (1d): We’re making Open USD the default for businesses using stablecoins on Stripe. Coming soon. [Likes: 40, Comments: 4]; **Jesse Carey** (6d): Shutdowns among new startups continue to decline. Our one-year shutdown proxy — the share of Stripe Atlas C corps whose registered agent service lapsed within a year of incorporation — has fallen to 27%, the lowest level since the VC winter of 2022. At the same time, Atlas incorporations increased 92%, and the share of founders reporting that they’re building AI products grew nearly 5x. Are AI startups finding more traction than skeptics expected, or are AI tools lowering the cost of building and extending startup runways? [Likes: 94, Comments: 11]; **Intercept** (1w): Today, we treat respiratory infections like the cold and flu as a minor nuisance. The evidence increasingly suggests otherwise. - Healthy people spend about 5% of their lives sick with respiratory infections. - Around 65 million respiratory infections progress to serious lower respiratory disease each year, accounting for around 7% of deaths from major causes in the U.S. - While research is early, it seems plausible that society has underestimated the long-term health implications of seemingly benign infections (e.g.: 9.8x asthma risk by age 6 if infected with HRV between birth and age 3 in a high-risk cohort; 2.2-3x schizophrenia potential risk for infant if mother is infected by flu during pregnancy). - Routine respiratory illness imposes roughly $600B global productivity loss in non-pandemic years. - Achieving broad protection against respiratory pathogens would meaningfully reduce pandemic risk. This is a challenging problem to solve, but new platform technologies, advances in our understanding of human immunology, biological data sets, and protein design tools mean we have our strongest ever suite of approaches for tackling it. We think two products working in tandem could meaningfully reduce this burden: - Broad-spectrum preventatives (i.e. a shot or pill that provide >90% protection against >90% of respiratory viruses) - Air cleaning technologies that remove pathogens from the air, particularly in high-density environments like offices, schools, and public transit. So today we’re launching Intercept, a $500M philanthropic initiative that aims to radically reduce the burden of respiratory infections, and eventually eliminate them altogether, by advancing these products through a combination of: - Grants and equity to de-risk early projects and advance them far enough for capital markets to kick in and take them the rest of the way. Anchor funders include Stripe , Anthropic , Flu Lab , The OpenAI Foundation , and individuals from Jane Street. - A customer advisory board of interested buyers who will provide important customer input to ensure the products being developed are the right ones. It includes Stripe , Anthropic , BXP, Inc. , Kilroy Realty Corporation , Jane Street , JPMorganChase , and Mastercard . - Engagement with regulators to accelerate the support and obtain the approvals required to bring both sets of products to the market. Respiratory infections aren't inevitable. If we can develop these technologies and deploy them at scale, the change would be profound. More information in the first comment. As Vice Chair, I'll represent the company with business, government, and policy leaders around the world, alongside Patrick Collison and John Collison . The internet economy is at an inflection point. Governments, regulators, and multilateral bodies are making once-in-a-generation decisions about how digital commerce is regulated and enabled—decisions that will set the operating conditions for entrepreneurs for decades. Stripe serves millions of businesses in nearly every country on earth. We have both the standing and the responsibility to shape those decisions. That's what I'll be doing: engaging heads of government, trade bodies, and global business leaders to advocate for decisions that advance entrepreneurship and increase the economic dynamism that too many parts of the world have been starved of. I've spent the last 25 years of my career building things, teams, markets, relationships. This next chapter is about using all of that on behalf of the businesses that trust Stripe to power their growth. As I start this new role, I'm delighted to have Tyler Bryson take over as Stripe's Chief Revenue Officer. Tyler brings two decades of experience building, scaling, and leading revenue-generating teams and has had a tremendous impact leading our Americas business. He knows our customers, understands what they need and we’re all very excited for his leadership as Stripe’s CRO. https://lnkd.in/e8cKgrwr [Likes: 3062, Comments: 338]; **Stripe** (1w): Introducing Stripe Directory, a new way for you (and your agents) to search for businesses on the Stripe network. https://stripe.directory [Likes: 153, Comments: 13]; **Stripe** (2w): In 2022, we launched Frontier to send a signal to scientists and entrepreneurs: build carbon removal technology, and we will buy it. In four years, the field went from a dozen or so companies to hundreds, removing tens of thousands of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere. Today, we are committing to buy an additional $915 million alongside Google , Shopify , Salesforce , H&M Group , and Anthropic . The technology works. The question now is whether demand can match the pace of technological progress. Frontier’s “Growth AMC” is designed to bridge that gap. Read more: https://lnkd.in/g-V3_FEA . [Likes: 141, Comments: 12]; **William Gaybrick** (2w): I just got off stage in Paris at Stripe Tour, talking about how French businesses are becoming more international. One in three customers of French businesses on Stripe now comes from outside France. French companies on Stripe generate 22% of their revenue internationally, up from 16% in 2020. Reaching customers in Mumbai or São Paulo, or giving them the option to pay later, means offering the payment methods they already use. That's where Link comes in. Just a couple of months ago we announced that Link surpassed 250 million users. Today I shared that it has more than 300 million, and supports Klarna, Pix, UPI, and stablecoins. More updates from Stripe Tour Paris: https://lnkd.in/gPYMrnZt . [Likes: 602, Comments: 19]; **Tanya Khakbaz** (2w): I was just at Stripe Tour Paris talking about a new frontier in fraud: token theft. Fraudsters have moved beyond stealing money and credentials — now they're stealing compute. Every prompt, every API call, every token costs real money. As AI gets embedded in more products, token theft is becoming one of the most urgent threats facing AI businesses. Here's everything we announced at Stripe Tour Paris: https://lnkd.in/gf4q-Fbs [Likes: 425, Comments: 31]; **Mikael Mello** (2w): I recently wrote about what I've been working on the past two years, and others have built over the past decade: the infrastructure that keeps Stripe's entire developer ecosystem in sync with every API change we ship. We built an OpenAPI-based pipeline that flows API changes from their initial definitions all the way to our SDKs, docs, and other developer products in lockstep, letting engineers focus on their product instead of manually propagating their changes to every developer product that Stripe offers. Read more about how it works under the hood → https://lnkd.in/dRJmwRVx [Likes: 166, Comments: 6]

Stripe is now a bank [several corrections and errors fixed, original post said stripe IS a bank, it has in fact, applied for a charter] Why? 1. It lets them control more of the software stack - They're not limited by what their bank partner can do. - They can manage risk with the data they see. 2. They receive funding from Visa/MasterCard directly - They can now own the merchant accounts to offer interest - When funds clear through the visanet and MasterCard networks, Stripe will collect that float directly. - Not "deposit taking" but tangential to merchant acquiring Stripe was clear they're not offering deposits but 3. I'm speculating this could be a precursor to them one day issuing working capital to SMEs from an ILC or similar arrangement. - They already offer Stripe Capital but they'd have strategic options here - They could start to offer more yield to merchants - They could issue their own stablecoin [Updated significantly thanks to [Bradley](https://www.linkedin.com/in/bradleyriss?trk=public_post-text) ] Stripe has applied to be a specific type of Acquiring bank are not like regular banks. The Georgia charter is one that typically only serve merchants and businesses. So no, Stripe isn't going to be a Nubank like consumer player because of this. I do imagine it gives them room to innovate longer term however.

Pretty wild: 60% of folks coming to Stripe from vibe coding platforms are creating new Stripe accounts. More and more people are building on AI powered code-generation platforms, but up until recently, adding payments still meant breaking flow: setting up accounts, wiring test environments, and context switching before you could charge a single customer. Stripe sandboxes now work natively inside those platforms, so you can set up payments where you build. A new generation of builders is creating new products, powered by AI (and Stripe!). Here’s how it works: [https://lnkd.in/gnUnWhEG](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FgnUnWhEG&urlhash=x1Xo&trk=public_post-text)

Just saw our story featured on Stripe's customer showcase! 🎉 What struck me most about our journey with Stripe's MCP (Model Context Protocol) was how quickly we went from idea to impact. In less than 5 minutes, we connected our AI agents to Stripe's payment data. But here's the real magic: what used to take our support team 30 mins per refund request (reviewing history, validating charges, drafting emails) now happens in seconds. The best part? We "ate our own dog food" first. Before rolling this out to customers, we used it internally—our "Dust for Dust" approach. This let us iron out the kinks and prove the value before sharing it with thousands of our users. Here's what I learned: AI isn't about replacing human judgment—it's about eliminating the time-consuming, low value steps so people can focus on what matters. Our agents still keep humans in the loop for validation, especially with sensitive financial operations. If you're curious about AI automation, start small. Pick one repetitive workflow that eats up your team's time. You might be surprised how much impact a simple automation can have. What's one workflow in your business that you wish could run itself? 👇

The tech industry is chasing a vanity metric. And I almost fell into the trap myself. When [Xinran](https://www.linkedin.com/in/xinran-he-17256850?trk=public_post-text), [Yuan](https://www.linkedin.com/in/yuan-bai-54206240?trk=public_post-text) and I started building, we were creating an LLM platform—chasing the hype of faster code generation. But our combined decades in the on-call trenches at Snap and Google tempered our perspective. We recognized a pattern the rest of the industry missed: 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗽. The 2025 DORA report confirms this. AI is speeding up coding, but system stability is decreasing by 7.2%. We’ve mistaken coding speed for delivery velocity. We’re accelerating development only to slam into an operational bottleneck. The time saved in creation is repaid, with interest, during incidents. The result is "comprehension debt"—trying to debug AI code you didn't write at 3 AM. As autonomous agents take over, this operational gap becomes critical. True velocity requires stability. That realization was the catalyst for [Bacca.ai](https://www.linkedin.com/company/bacca-ai?trk=public_post-text). We need to stop obsessing over the first mile and start solving for the last. My full philosophy on the Velocity Trap in the comments.

# Stripe OLT
The Microsoft Cloud & Cyber Security Specialists - A Littlefish Group Company
IT Services and IT Consulting • Bristol, Bristol • 6,170 followers • 51-200 employees

## Overview
From our offices in London, Bristol, and Manchester, Stripe OLT delivers cutting-edge cyber security and IT services to support and protect organisations in an ever-changing digital world. As part of the Littlefish Group, we combine the agility and expertise of a specialist cyber security provider with the scale and capability of a leading managed IT services organisation. With our highly-certified 24/7 Security Operations Centre (SOC) and IT Helpdesk, we deliver reliable protection and support, safeguarding critical UK infrastructure while optimising efficiency and reducing business costs. Recognised as a Top 32 Scale-Up by Business Leader and a Megabyte Top 50 Rising Star, we’ve been winning awards year-on-year since 2021, because we’re backed by a team dedicated to excellence. At Stripe OLT, we believe in pushing boundaries to deliver exceptional results—because when we perform at our best, our clients can focus on what they do best. www.stripeolt.com | hello@stripeolt.com | 0207 043 7044

Early [Stripe](https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe?trk=public_post-text)s, Where Are They Now? [Patrick Collison](https://www.linkedin.com/in/patrickcollison?trk=public_post-text) and [John Collison](https://www.linkedin.com/in/johnbcollison?trk=public_post-text) personally interviewed every single candidate for years. You had to pass a bar that most companies would never set Where are they now? Using the Crustdata API, I pulled a collection of early [Stripe](https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe?trk=public_post-text) employees that helped build the first version of Stripe: [Anurag Goel](https://www.linkedin.com/in/anuragoel?trk=public_post-text) joined in August 2011 as Head of Risk, building the fraud systems that let Stripe handle real money at scale without getting destroyed by bad actors. He left in 2016 and founded [Render](https://www.linkedin.com/company/renderco?trk=public_post-text), now used by 5M+ developers as their cloud platform [Saikat Chakrabarti](https://www.linkedin.com/in/saikatc?trk=public_post-text) joined in February 2011 as a Founding Engineer, one of the first people to write production code at Stripe. He quit tech entirely, managed [Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for Congress](https://www.linkedin.com/company/aocforcongress?trk=public_post-text) congressional campaign, became her Chief of Staff, and is now running for Congress himself in CA-11 (so casual haha) [Amber Feng](https://www.linkedin.com/in/amberfeng?trk=public_post-text) joined in January 2012 as a Product Engineer and grew all the way to Head of Financial Infrastructure, the team responsible for Stripe's Treasury and banking products. She later co-founded [Cocoon](https://www.linkedin.com/company/meetcocoon?trk=public_post-text) as CTO. [Alex MacCaw](https://www.linkedin.com/in/alex-maccaw-ab592978?trk=public_post-text) joined in January 2012 as an Engineer, came from [Twitter](https://www.linkedin.com/company/twitter?trk=public_post-text), stayed one year, then left to build [Clearbit](https://www.linkedin.com/company/clearbit?trk=public_post-text) from scratch. [Clearbit](https://www.linkedin.com/company/clearbit?trk=public_post-text) became the standard for B2B data enrichment and sold to [HubSpot](https://www.linkedin.com/company/hubspot?trk=public_post-text). He is now CEO at [Reflect](https://fr.linkedin.com/company/reflect-hr?trk=public_post-text)& building something new [Benjamin Rahn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/benrahn?trk=public_post-text) joined in January 2012 as a Software Engineer and stayed 8 years, making Staff Engineer. He is now Founder and board member at [ActBlue](https://www.linkedin.com/company/actblue?trk=public_post-text), the platform behind most major Democratic campaign fundraising in the US [Lachy Groom](https://www.linkedin.com/in/lachy-groom-b218895?trk=public_post-text) joined in January 2012 and spent 7 years building Stripe Issuing, the product that lets companies spin up their own card programs. He left in 2018 and is now Co-Founder at [Physical Intelligence](https://www.linkedin.com/company/physical-intelligence?trk=public_post-text), one of the most watched robotics AI labs right now [Timothy Thairu](https://ke.linkedin.com/in/thairu?trk=public_post-text) joined in April 2012 as an Engineer, coming from 6 years at [Microsoft](https://www.linkedin.com/company/microsoft?trk=public_post-text). He stayed 7 years building core infrastructure at Stripe [Michael Schade](https://www.linkedin.com/in/michaelschade?trk=public_post-text) joined in April 2012 as Head of Support, then moved into engineering as Head of Leverage Engineering. He later founded [Kenchi](https://www.linkedin.com/company/kenchi?trk=public_post-text), then joined [OpenAI](https://www.linkedin.com/company/openai?trk=public_post-text) where he is now Strategic Projects Lead (where he joins another Early Stripe Employee, [Greg Brockman](https://www.linkedin.com/in/thegdb?trk=public_post-text) Which company should we look at next? One graph from Stripe Sessions this week stopped me cold... AI agents are on track to read more Stripe documentation than human developers. That. Is. Wild. Your next "developer" might not have a GitHub profile. It might not attend your conference. It will never watch your YouTube tutorial. But it will consume your API docs, your schema definitions, and your error codes at machine speed. This isn't a prediction; this isn't a future possibility. Stripe is seeing it happen in real time. And I think this fundamentally changes how we need to think about Developer Experience and driving awareness to your documentation. At Nokia, we have already been thinking about this exact shift with Network as Code (see comments for more information) Our network APIs (number verification, SIM swap detection, device location, quality on demand) were originally built for human developers to integrate. But the next wave of consumption is going to be agents discovering and calling these APIs autonomously. Agents will be building services to perform fraud checks, identity verification, and network-aware decision making, and we are building for exactly that. The companies that design their APIs, docs, and developer experience for agent-first consumption are going to win the next decade. The ones that don't will wonder why their traffic flatlined while usage exploded somewhere else. What does "agent-first developer experience" even look like? I think we're all still figuring that out. What a week at [Stripe](https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe?trk=public_post-text) Sessions. Many highlights for me, and even more ideas and issues to reflect on. Here are just a few: 🤖 The topic of the week was, of course, AI. The main debate seemed to center on the pace of adoption--whether the frictions that have caused prior technological revolutions to embed themselves in the economy only over long periods of time will prevail. We have clearly passed some kind of tipping point, with new business formation, startup revenue and global growth, and of course AI code generation all racing past any prior benchmarks. 💲 I moderated a panel on stablecoins and how regulation will inflect adoption. Tremendous insights from [Katie Biber](https://www.linkedin.com/in/katiebiber?trk=public_post-text), [Ondřej Kovařík](https://be.linkedin.com/in/okovarik?trk=public_post-text), and [John Tullis](https://www.linkedin.com/in/johnrtullis?trk=public_post-text) on the role that regulation is playing in giving established companies like [Gusto](https://www.linkedin.com/company/gustohq?trk=public_post-text) the confidence to incorporate stablecoins into global payouts. We also discussed what regulators will have to get right in the US and elsewhere--including assuring a competitive marketplace, and building mutual recognition frameworks to avoid erecting regulatory borders around this borderless technology. ✒️ The craft and beauty with which the Stripe design and marketing teams built the entire conference experience. It was an *experience* just to be there, and a delight to notice the many small details that created such richness. It was also a treat to see so many of my colleagues in person, many for the first time, and to catch up with old friends and colleagues. Till next time!

[Stripe](https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe?trk=public_post-text) merges over a thousand pull requests a week that no human wrote, inside a codebase that moves a trillion dollars a year. They did not buy an agent. They built the environment around it. A “minion” is kicked off from a Slack thread. Ten seconds later it is inside an isolated devbox, pre-loaded with Stripe's code and services, reading the thread as context. It writes, runs CI, and returns a PR. Stripe forked Block's goose, pointed it at an internal MCP server with 400+ tools, and gave the agents the same tooling their engineers use. [Alistair Gray](https://www.linkedin.com/in/%7Ealistair?trk=public_post-text) is walking through how they built it at the Background Agents Summit on 6 May. If you want to see what this actually looks like at scale, come for this talk on 6 May. Still processing this week in San Francisco. Stripe Sessions was honestly one of those experiences that leaves you both in awe and re-energized. There’s something very different about reading where AI, payments and infrastructure are going vs. being in the room with people who are actually shaping that future. A few ideas I’m taking back with me: From Sam Altman’s chat, a big reminder that the Age of AI is not only about models or software. Material science, energy, chips and the physical infrastructure behind all of this are going to matter a lot. Also, the more developers build and launch with AI, the more important developer experience becomes. The companies that help builders move faster, with more control and less friction, are going to be in a very interesting place. At DigitalOcean Deploy, I loved how practical some of the conversations were. Especially around managing LLM budgets better, understanding output tokens, and designing systems that don’t just feel impressive, but are actually sustainable to operate. And in conversations with different leaders, one thing kept coming up: AI is already changing the world of services. Front desk operations, customer intake, support, follow-up, internal coordination. So many workflows are about to be redesigned. I came back with a lot of notes, a lot of ideas, and a refreshed sense of urgency. Amazing experience. Grateful to have been there, and excited to keep building.

Spent the day yesterday at Stripe Sessions in SF. Sam Altman was surprise guest. Fired off some awkward jokes about the Elon trial, obvi. And some rando interrupted the talk to protest AI. Pretty routine stuff for a Sam Altman interview. One interesting part was his prediction for what OpenAI's business would look 10 years from now. He basically said frontier labs might start looking more like utilities. Lower margins but at a scale that's almost impossible to comprehend. Cheaper, faster, better intelligence delivered instantly to anyone across the globe. The math works because the volume is, as he says, "uncapped." That ubiquity dismantles legacy software. Big headcount, slow release cycles, products built for a different decade. The margin math is simply changing. There's always going to be a small, nimble team armed with Claude ready to undercut the market. No headcount, no real estate, no GTM org to feed. They'll charge pennies on the dollar and still run a great business. If your model only works at legacy margins, your model might quickly become your biggest problem. If you're in build mode, you're used to the new normal. Roadmaps are now organized by week, or even by day. It's what it takes to survive. Anthropic and OpenAI have completely reset market expectations. Sam said the industry changes meaningfully every single week, and for the emerging leaders output has gone up exponentially while software cycles have collapsed. Strange thing to sit with. But it's the environment now. If you're not moving with the same urgency as the Claude and Codex teams, you better come up with a plan fast. Your competitors are shipping in a day or two what used to take a quarter at your run-of-the-mill 2015 SaaS company. The most dangerous thing right now is being disillusioned about where you actually stand. Don't assume your team is on the train because they showed you a fancy library of .md files and some non-technical folks pushed a few PRs.   The 7 lines of code that turned Stripe into a $95B company (while others failed) In 2010, accepting online payments was so complex it required: • 3+ weeks of engineering time • Multiple bank approvals • Security compliance headaches • Custom integration work Dozens of payment startups were adding features, creating "full-solution platforms" to solve this. But Patrick and John Collison made the opposite decision: They created a payment API requiring just 7 lines of code. When customers asked for features, they refused and doubled down on simplicity. Their "7-line" strategy seemed crazy but created 3 advantages: 1. Integration moat: By controlling the full payment stack (not outsourcing), they delivered 99.99% uptime while competitors suffered outages 3. Enterprise foundation: The simple API actually scaled better for large customers, enabling Stripe to move upmarket while feature-focused competitors got stuck downmarket The results: • 2010: 7-line MVP • 2011: $2M in funding • 2016: Processing billions monthly • 2021: $95B valuation • 2024: Powers >50% of online businesses Meanwhile, dozens of well-funded competitors with "more features" failed. Personal update: I’m joining [Stripe](https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe?trk=public_post-text) next month as Head of Design and I couldn't be more excited! I’ll be leading a talented team across brand, product, research, publishing, and more. I've always admired them afar and it's a true honor to be counted among them! Stripe has blown me away with their bold long-term thinking and awesome ability to execute swiftly. Everyone I've met is highly skilled and driven, yet humble and curious—with exceedingly high standards and devotion to constant improvement. While Stripe is well on its way to being a generation-defining company, it's still early days. The mission to increase the GDP of the internet couldn't be more salient than it is today and we look forward to helping build a new (and better) normal that enables greater access and prosperity globally. I am thrilled to be a part of Stripe in this journey! In addition, I will continue my work on [Benetech](https://www.linkedin.com/company/benetech?trk=public_post-text)'s board of directors and my advisory work with @GVDesignTeam and others. There's so much great work going on every which way. Just leave it to a hard year to tease out the best in innovation!

Stripe Link Moving on Up While Stripe Link has been quiet for a long time, it does appear that the profile of the payment method is increasing. Stripe is hiring for a Head of Consumer Marketing for Link on its website. Reported facts include: \* Over 100 million consumers \* Millions more joining the network each month That compares to 200M+ Shop Pay users (as reported in Feb by Shopify). It seems to me that Stripe Link is growing about 2x slower than Shop Pay -- at least on an order of magnitude -- and that Stripe would like to accelerate that. While I can compare it to Shop Pay here, the real issue is Paypal. With a consumer-facing arm, Paypal has many more weapons to win a long-term war than Stripe does. So Stripe Link growth rates matter. However, Stripe and Shopify and Paypal while overlapping and all are competing, they are also not 100% in competition -- likely all CEOs feel there can be multiple winners here.... so again, growth rates matter. And while Paypal Branded Checkout is growing much slower than Shopify, it's also growing slower than Stripe Link too. Meaning ... Stripe wouldn't mind increasing its growth rate here. Over the long term if you are close to the consumer you have more opportunities to increase your margin through ads, lending and other means than the alternative.

  💥 The Payment App Plot Twist It always starts the same way. A client pays you — PayPal, Stripe, Venmo, Zelle, Square, Apple Pay, Shopify, Etsy… The money hits your bank. You celebrate. 🥳 Life is good… until January. Your Profit & Loss looks suspiciously too good. You stare at the numbers thinking — “I swear I didn’t make that much.” 😳 Somewhere in your books, your income has doubled itself. And that, my friends, is how the Payment App Plot Twist begins. 💀 🧾 How to Record Payments Without Losing Your Mind: 💳 PayPal / Stripe / Venmo / Square / Cash App / Shopify / Etsy 1️⃣ Record the full sale → e.g. $100 income. 2️⃣ Record the processing fee → e.g. $3 expense. 3️⃣ Match the net deposit ($97) to your bank feed. 💡 Don’t record it twice. One sale, one fee, one clean match. 🧠 Pro tip: If you sell through Shopify or Etsy, those platforms act just like Stripe or PayPal — they hold the payment, take their fee, then send what’s left. Set up a clearing account or reconciliation process so your sales, fees, and deposits actually make sense later. And if you’re thinking, “Wait, what’s a clearing account?” — don’t worry, that’s exactly tomorrow’s drama. 😏 🏦 Zelle The calm one. No middleman. No fees. If $100 hits your bank → record $100 income and move on. ✅ 🍎 Apple Pay / Samsung Pay / Google Pay The sneaky ones. They’re not processors — just digital wallets. If the money goes straight to your bank, treat it like Zelle. If it goes through Stripe, Square, or Shopify first, treat it like Stripe. 💡 Always follow where the money actually lands, not what button your customer pressed. 💸 But wait — what if you use these apps to buy something for your business? Simple rule: Record what you bought, not how you paid for it. 🖨️ Paid for printer ink via PayPal? → Office Supplies. 🧾 Paid a contractor through Venmo? → Contractor Expense. 💻 Paid your Canva or Shopify subscription through Stripe? → Software Expense. 🚗 Bought gas using Apple Pay? → Auto/Travel Expense. PayPal, Venmo, or Zelle are just payment methods, not expense categories. Because clean books aren’t about perfection — they’re about survival. 😅 And when tax season hits, the only drama you want is whether you’ll need one cup of coffee or three. ☕☕☕ 💬 Tomorrow’s sequel: 🎬 “Clearing Account vs. Uncategorized: The Great Bookkeeping Showdown.” Same drama. More clarity. Fewer mystery transactions. 💭 Your turn: Which app causes the biggest chaos in your books — PayPal, Stripe, Shopify, Etsy, Zelle, or the mysterious “Apple Pay deposit”? Globally, [Stripe](https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe?trk=public_post-text) processed transactions generated $𝟭.𝟰 𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 in total payment volume in 2024, which is equal to about 1.3% of global GDP 🤯 There are more interesting Stripe Statistics: 👉 Stripe generated $1.4 trillion in total payment volume in 2024, up 38% from the prior year. 👉 Merchants in 50 countries use Stripe to accept and process payments. 👉 More than 100 Stripe customers process $1 billion or more yearly (up from 40 in 2020). 👉 4,776,230 million websites have used Stripe to accept payment. 👉 Stripe is currently valued at $91,5 billion, making it one of the most valuable privately-held companies on the planet. 👉 Stripe’s market share dropped from 21% to 17.15%, yet it remains the world's second most used payment solution. They're building the rails for agentic commerce – where AI agents make payment decisions autonomously. Here's what this means for payment recovery: When I started in this space, failed payments were a "retry later" problem. You'd ping the same card, same way, hoping it worked the second time. Now? AI agents can: •Analyze why a payment failed in real-time •Switch payment methods intelligently •Optimize retry timing based on customer behavior •Even negotiate payment plans autonomously The $106.7 billion bet isn't on faster buttons or smarter wallets. It's on invisible payments that just work. Last week, one of our clients saw their payment recovery rate jump from 62% to 78% – not because they changed their payment processor, but because they let AI agents handle the decision-making. The future of payments isn't what we click. It's what we never have to think about. What do you think? Are we ready for a world where payments become completely invisible? # Stripe's shipping pace: a lesson in execution discipline

This title was summarized by AI from the post below.

[Alison Lange Engel](https://www.linkedin.com/in/alisonlangeengel?trk=public_post_feed-actor-name)

CEO / CMO (Stripe, LinkedIn) / Investor / Advisor

* [Report this post](/uas/login?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Fposts%2Falisonlangeengel_the-pace-of-shipping-at-stripe-is-just-awesome-activity-7381721932746067968-QRRv&trk=public_post_ellipsis-menu-semaphore-sign-in-redirect&guestReportContentType=POST&_f=guest-reporting)

The pace of shipping at [Stripe](https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe?trk=public_post-text) is just awesome to see. How scaled tech companies continue to ruthlessly prioritize exceptional product and user experience is a lesson for everyone. There are many posts here about driving execution discipline within your company. As a CEO or team leader, we can talk about it all day long. The outcome is in the doing. And the discipline of sticking to the doing above all else.

[Steve Kaliski](https://www.linkedin.com/in/steve-kaliski-079a7710?trk=public_post_reshare_feed-actor-name)

Principal Software Engineer at Stripe

My absolute favorite thing about Stripe is that even 15 years and thousands of employees in, we can still mobilize in the snap of a finger. What went from some prototyping, demos, and noodling, turned quickly into 100s of Stripes sprinting to help power Instant Checkout in ChatGPT. It was the most rewarding and intense work I’ve had the pleasure of doing at Stripe. Incredible focus and momentum from the team. The product is incredibly simple – write your prompt, find products, click buy. But under the hood we had to solve tons of problems. The checkout experience as a buyer no longer lives on the seller’s site. We had to figure out how to generate and securely share payment credentials and define open standards for Agent<->Seller checkout. And most critically, we wanted to make this incredibly easy for sellers – as little as one line change to how you process your existing payments on Stripe. When speaking to users, we knew they were looking for actionable steps – “show me the integration guide” – and so that’s what we did. We co-designed the Agentic Commerce Protocol with OpenAI to provide concrete steps for sellers to make their checkouts agent ready, and we launched Stripe’s Shared Payment Token to enable agents and sellers to securely transit payment credentials with usage limits for 100s of payment methods. Learn more at [https://lnkd.in/eJvcD8\_B](https://lnkd.in/eJvcD8_B?trk=public_post_reshare-text) and [https://lnkd.in/eCrK2J8y](https://lnkd.in/eCrK2J8y?trk=public_post_reshare-text).

If you rely on Stripe, this update is more than a version change and marks a clear shift in how businesses build with it. Stripe has introduced a new release model with major updates twice a year and smaller ones every month. These updates have changed how APIs respond, how webhooks are triggered, and how data objects behave. If your integration has not been updated recently, you might be missing new features or facing hidden issues caused by outdated SDKs. The brighter side is that Stripe has become smarter.   💡 PaymentIntent vs. SetupIntent — what’s the real difference? If you’ve ever integrated Stripe, you’ve probably seen both — but their purpose is often misunderstood 👇 💰 PaymentIntent → used when you want to collect money now. It represents the process of confirming and capturing a payment (e.g., checkout). 💳 SetupIntent → used when you want to save a payment method for future use. It authorizes and verifies a card without charging it. In short: 🧾 PaymentIntent = Pay now 💡 SetupIntent = Save for later Understanding this difference helps you design smoother, more secure checkout flows — especially for subscriptions, pre-orders, and one-click payments. # Early Stripe Employees: Where Are They Now

This title was summarized by AI from the post below.

[![Image 2: View profile for Sarah Chan](https://media.licdn.com/dms/image/v2/D4E03AQHYmDlG3FBUJg/profile-displayphoto-scale_400_400/B4EZv_pmDYI0Ag-/0/1769520652976?e=2147483647&v=beta&t=uGgN0Di21E3JM782FxuV04Ix67yP0BIr2WQI4AWEPf0)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sarahchan25?trk=public_post_feed-actor-image)

 4w  Edited

Early [Stripe](https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe?trk=public_post-text)s, Where Are They Now? [Patrick Collison](https://www.linkedin.com/in/patrickcollison?trk=public_post-text) and [John Collison](https://www.linkedin.com/in/johnbcollison?trk=public_post-text) personally interviewed every single candidate for years. You had to pass a bar that most companies would never set Where are they now? Using the Crustdata API, I pulled a collection of early [Stripe](https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe?trk=public_post-text) employees that helped build the first version of Stripe: [Anurag Goel](https://www.linkedin.com/in/anuragoel?trk=public_post-text) joined in August 2011 as Head of Risk, building the fraud systems that let Stripe handle real money at scale without getting destroyed by bad actors. He left in 2016 and founded [Render](https://www.linkedin.com/company/renderco?trk=public_post-text), now used by 5M+ developers as their cloud platform [Saikat Chakrabarti](https://www.linkedin.com/in/saikatc?trk=public_post-text) joined in February 2011 as a Founding Engineer, one of the first people to write production code at Stripe. He quit tech entirely, managed [Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for Congress](https://www.linkedin.com/company/aocforcongress?trk=public_post-text) congressional campaign, became her Chief of Staff, and is now running for Congress himself in CA-11 (so casual haha) [Amber Feng](https://www.linkedin.com/in/amberfeng?trk=public_post-text) joined in January 2012 as a Product Engineer and grew all the way to Head of Financial Infrastructure, the team responsible for Stripe's Treasury and banking products. She later co-founded [Cocoon](https://www.linkedin.com/company/meetcocoon?trk=public_post-text) as CTO. [Alex MacCaw](https://www.linkedin.com/in/alex-maccaw-ab592978?trk=public_post-text) joined in January 2012 as an Engineer, came from [Twitter](https://www.linkedin.com/company/twitter?trk=public_post-text), stayed one year, then left to build [Clearbit](https://www.linkedin.com/company/clearbit?trk=public_post-text) from scratch. [Clearbit](https://www.linkedin.com/company/clearbit?trk=public_post-text) became the standard for B2B data enrichment and sold to [HubSpot](https://www.linkedin.com/company/hubspot?trk=public_post-text). He is now CEO at [Reflect](https://fr.linkedin.com/company/reflect-hr?trk=public_post-text)& building something new [Benjamin Rahn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/benrahn?trk=public_post-text) joined in January 2012 as a Software Engineer and stayed 8 years, making Staff Engineer. He is now Founder and board member at [ActBlue](https://www.linkedin.com/company/actblue?trk=public_post-text), the platform behind most major Democratic campaign fundraising in the US [Lachy Groom](https://www.linkedin.com/in/lachy-groom-b218895?trk=public_post-text) joined in January 2012 and spent 7 years building Stripe Issuing, the product that lets companies spin up their own card programs. He left in 2018 and is now Co-Founder at [Physical Intelligence](https://www.linkedin.com/company/physical-intelligence?trk=public_post-text), one of the most watched robotics AI labs right now [Timothy Thairu](https://ke.linkedin.com/in/thairu?trk=public_post-text) joined in April 2012 as an Engineer, coming from 6 years at [Microsoft](https://www.linkedin.com/company/microsoft?trk=public_post-text). He stayed 7 years building core infrastructure at Stripe [Michael Schade](https://www.linkedin.com/in/michaelschade?trk=public_post-text) joined in April 2012 as Head of Support, then moved into engineering as Head of Leverage Engineering. He later founded [Kenchi](https://www.linkedin.com/company/kenchi?trk=public_post-text), then joined [OpenAI](https://www.linkedin.com/company/openai?trk=public_post-text) where he is now Strategic Projects Lead (where he joins another Early Stripe Employee, [Greg Brockman](https://www.linkedin.com/in/thegdb?trk=public_post-text) Which company should we look at next? One graph from Stripe Sessions this week stopped me cold... AI agents are on track to read more Stripe documentation than human developers. That. Is. Wild. Your next "developer" might not have a GitHub profile. It might not attend your conference. It will never watch your YouTube tutorial. But it will consume your API docs, your schema definitions, and your error codes at machine speed. This isn't a prediction; this isn't a future possibility. Stripe is seeing it happen in real time. And I think this fundamentally changes how we need to think about Developer Experience and driving awareness to your documentation. At Nokia, we have already been thinking about this exact shift with Network as Code (see comments for more information) Our network APIs (number verification, SIM swap detection, device location, quality on demand) were originally built for human developers to integrate. But the next wave of consumption is going to be agents discovering and calling these APIs autonomously. Agents will be building services to perform fraud checks, identity verification, and network-aware decision making, and we are building for exactly that. The companies that design their APIs, docs, and developer experience for agent-first consumption are going to win the next decade. The ones that don't will wonder why their traffic flatlined while usage exploded somewhere else. What does "agent-first developer experience" even look like? I think we're all still figuring that out. What a week at [Stripe](https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe?trk=public_post-text) Sessions. Many highlights for me, and even more ideas and issues to reflect on. Here are just a few: 🤖 The topic of the week was, of course, AI. The main debate seemed to center on the pace of adoption--whether the frictions that have caused prior technological revolutions to embed themselves in the economy only over long periods of time will prevail. We have clearly passed some kind of tipping point, with new business formation, startup revenue and global growth, and of course AI code generation all racing past any prior benchmarks. 💲 I moderated a panel on stablecoins and how regulation will inflect adoption. Tremendous insights from [Katie Biber](https://www.linkedin.com/in/katiebiber?trk=public_post-text), [Ondřej Kovařík](https://be.linkedin.com/in/okovarik?trk=public_post-text), and [John Tullis](https://www.linkedin.com/in/johnrtullis?trk=public_post-text) on the role that regulation is playing in giving established companies like [Gusto](https://www.linkedin.com/company/gustohq?trk=public_post-text) the confidence to incorporate stablecoins into global payouts. We also discussed what regulators will have to get right in the US and elsewhere--including assuring a competitive marketplace, and building mutual recognition frameworks to avoid erecting regulatory borders around this borderless technology. ✒️ The craft and beauty with which the Stripe design and marketing teams built the entire conference experience. It was an *experience* just to be there, and a delight to notice the many small details that created such richness. It was also a treat to see so many of my colleagues in person, many for the first time, and to catch up with old friends and colleagues. Till next time!

[Stripe](https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe?trk=public_post-text) merges over a thousand pull requests a week that no human wrote, inside a codebase that moves a trillion dollars a year. They did not buy an agent. They built the environment around it. A “minion” is kicked off from a Slack thread. Ten seconds later it is inside an isolated devbox, pre-loaded with Stripe's code and services, reading the thread as context. It writes, runs CI, and returns a PR. Stripe forked Block's goose, pointed it at an internal MCP server with 400+ tools, and gave the agents the same tooling their engineers use. [Alistair Gray](https://www.linkedin.com/in/%7Ealistair?trk=public_post-text) is walking through how they built it at the Background Agents Summit on 6 May. If you want to see what this actually looks like at scale, come for this talk on 6 May. Still processing this week in San Francisco. Stripe Sessions was honestly one of those experiences that leaves you both in awe and re-energized. There’s something very different about reading where AI, payments and infrastructure are going vs. being in the room with people who are actually shaping that future. A few ideas I’m taking back with me: From Sam Altman’s chat, a big reminder that the Age of AI is not only about models or software. Material science, energy, chips and the physical infrastructure behind all of this are going to matter a lot. Also, the more developers build and launch with AI, the more important developer experience becomes. The companies that help builders move faster, with more control and less friction, are going to be in a very interesting place. At DigitalOcean Deploy, I loved how practical some of the conversations were. Especially around managing LLM budgets better, understanding output tokens, and designing systems that don’t just feel impressive, but are actually sustainable to operate. And in conversations with different leaders, one thing kept coming up: AI is already changing the world of services. Front desk operations, customer intake, support, follow-up, internal coordination. So many workflows are about to be redesigned. I came back with a lot of notes, a lot of ideas, and a refreshed sense of urgency. Amazing experience. Grateful to have been there, and excited to keep building.

Spent the day yesterday at Stripe Sessions in SF. Sam Altman was surprise guest. Fired off some awkward jokes about the Elon trial, obvi. And some rando interrupted the talk to protest AI. Pretty routine stuff for a Sam Altman interview. One interesting part was his prediction for what OpenAI's business would look 10 years from now. He basically said frontier labs might start looking more like utilities. Lower margins but at a scale that's almost impossible to comprehend. Cheaper, faster, better intelligence delivered instantly to anyone across the globe. The math works because the volume is, as he says, "uncapped." That ubiquity dismantles legacy software. Big headcount, slow release cycles, products built for a different decade. The margin math is simply changing. There's always going to be a small, nimble team armed with Claude ready to undercut the market. No headcount, no real estate, no GTM org to feed. They'll charge pennies on the dollar and still run a great business. If your model only works at legacy margins, your model might quickly become your biggest problem. If you're in build mode, you're used to the new normal. Roadmaps are now organized by week, or even by day. It's what it takes to survive. Anthropic and OpenAI have completely reset market expectations. Sam said the industry changes meaningfully every single week, and for the emerging leaders output has gone up exponentially while software cycles have collapsed. Strange thing to sit with. But it's the environment now. If you're not moving with the same urgency as the Claude and Codex teams, you better come up with a plan fast. Your competitors are shipping in a day or two what used to take a quarter at your run-of-the-mill 2015 SaaS company. The most dangerous thing right now is being disillusioned about where you actually stand. Don't assume your team is on the train because they showed you a fancy library of .md files and some non-technical folks pushed a few PRs. The speed of innovation right now should 100% blow your mind. If it doesn't, you gotta start asking the hard questions.

We think two products working in tandem could meaningfully reduce this burden: - Broad-spectrum preventatives (i.e. a shot or pill that provide >90% protection against >90% of respiratory viruses) - Air cleaning technologies that remove pathogens from the air, particularly in high-density environments like offices, schools, and public transit. Lessons from Stripe's early days: intensity, manual work, and urgency
=====================================================================

This title was summarized by AI from the post below.

[![Image 2: View profile for Elise Pham](https://media.licdn.com/dms/image/v2/D5603AQGQfbY5b9LpuA/profile-displayphoto-scale_400_400/B56ZpQ4MCoJ4Ak-/0/1762293499483?e=2147483647&v=beta&t=hTafeSpBmpZodlB8LQuu87hrUHytF_6hDtmfJMfVtAU)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/elise-pham-8112821b0?trk=public_post_feed-actor-image)

 3mo

Most people know [Stripe](https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe?trk=public_post-text) as a $65B+ fintech giant. I sat down with employee #1 and here’s what I learned: 1. Density of intensity matters more than headcount. A few people fully committed and pushing each other will outpace a much larger, diluted team 2. Do the manual work before you automate. Early Stripe kept processes hands-on longer than competitors to extract insights, build respect, and ensure everyone’s contribution mattered. 3. Urgency is contagious. Even in small, “unimportant” tasks, Stripe’s culture was about doing it now, not later. And that habit compounded into speed. Thank you [Darragh Buckley](https://www.linkedin.com/in/darragh-buckley-56096312?trk=public_post-text) for showing that team culture is built in the small moments, and those moments can scale into something massive 🏆

Years ago, I flubbed an interview with Stripe's cofounder John Collison. I was fresh off a tough job. The things I was still processing in that conversation killed any chance I had: At the time, Stripe wasn’t even sure they wanted product management. I made it easy for them to pass. Looking back, I wouldn’t have hired that version of me either. After interviewing thousands of people across functions, I often see the same patterns. They make me cringe at the obvious ways I was shooting myself in the foot. 1. Showing up wounded. We're all human and have been through things. Sure you can use that to be real and show you’ve learned. But more often it looks like you’re still processing. Why draft a player who’s still injured over one at full health? 2. Lack of (grounded) confidence. If you don't know you're good, why will someone else? Don’t mistake this for hubris. That loses too. Instead, be clear about what you bring, based on real results. 3. Energy is contagious. People mirror what they see. If you’re curious and excited, you’re more likely to get the same back and they’ll like you more. 4. The biggest mistake: not letting them know you want the job. Candidates think playing hard to get is strategic. Of course you’re evaluating them too. Good people have options. But everyone wants to be chosen. Literally saying "I want this job" increases your odds of getting it. Share what excites you about the role. Be enthusiastic about the parts you love. Nobody wants to work with someone who doesn't want to work with them. You already know all of this. You've probably given the same advice to someone else. But if you’re not landing your dream job, you’re still making these mistakes yourself. Getting out of your own way is harder than it sounds. Trust me, I’ve been there.

First day as a founder vs. 5 years later. Still convinced this is all I want to do for the rest of my life. A few things I learned: I was wrong about almost everything. You don’t build a company once, you rebuild it every quarter. The setup that got you started won’t survive later. Every system breaks the moment you scale it. And nobody claps when you fix it. The bar just moves higher. After a while, you realize your job is to build systems 24/7. To find leverage when sleep is short and runway is shorter. To sell something you still believe in after the 200,000 rejections. Then you learn the most painful truth: What you built for your first 1K customers isn’t what your next 10K will need. You have to throw out everything you believe in again and again. Your assumptions. Your roadmap. Your entire source of truth. Because data from yesterday’s users rarely maps to tomorrow’s growth. The trick isn’t to abandon what got you here, it’s to protect the core of why your first customers believed in you, and then keep evolving the layers of value you provide. Stripe did it perfectly: They started with one job: accept payments. Then added analytics. Reporting. Reconciliation. Fraud tools. Until their ecosystem of value became the moat. Even if someone builds a better feature, they can’t beat the total experience. That’s the lesson: 1:1 thinking only gets you so far. Iteration compounds. Ecosystems win. The whole game is about staying alive long enough to compound. Or about replacing chaos with systems. And about finding peace in the uncertainty you signed up for. Most people think founders are dreamers. The truth is, we’re just the ones too stubborn to quit. We break things. We rebuild. We repeat. And somewhere between the late nights, empty rooms, and broken systems, you realize you didn’t just build a company. You built yourself. > Share this if someone needs to hear this. > Follow me, [Catalin Fetean](https://ro.linkedin.com/in/catalinfetean?trk=public_post-text) for more.

Stripe had only 50 users after 2 years. Here’s the Growth Formula that turned it into a $90 billion company: Hack # 1 Instead of sharing a signup link, they installed Stripe for founders manually. Hack # 2 They used the YC network loop. Every time one YC-startup founder installed Stripe, others asked, “Wait… how are you taking payments so easily?” Hack # 3 Stripe was invite-only. Scarcity = Signal. # Mike Mahlkow’s Post

[Mike Mahlkow](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mikemahlkow?trk=public_post_feed-actor-name)

* [Report this post](/uas/login?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Fposts%2Fmikemahlkow_when-i-joined-stripe-in-2018-i-learned-a-activity-7417020311939960832-EmA5&trk=public_post_ellipsis-menu-semaphore-sign-in-redirect&guestReportContentType=POST&_f=guest-reporting)

When I joined Stripe in 2018, I learned a lot about how great companies are run from the inside. One small but memorable detail: every new employee received a copy of The Dream Machine. The book tells the story of how personal computing came to be, driven not by a founder or an engineer, but by one of the most important visionaries of the 20th century: J. C. R. Licklider. He didn’t write code or start a company. He still shaped how an entire generation thought about computers, networks, and humans working together. I could not help but be inspired by a company that provides employees with one of the best books on computing history ever written as a welcome gift. If you care about technology, innovation, or the people behind foundational ideas, this book belongs at the very top of your reading list. For anyone who wants to go deeper, here’s my personal shortlist of great books on the history of computing, ordered roughly by the periods they cover: • The Innovators (Walter Isaacson) | 1840s to today A people-first history from Ada Lovelace to the modern internet. A great high-level primer and a good place to start. • The Idea Factory (Jon Gertner) | 1920s to 1980s How Bell Labs repeatedly produced world-changing breakthroughs and what made that environment work. • The Dream Machine (M. Mitchell Waldrop) | 1950s to 1970s The intellectual origins of interactive computing, networking, and personal computers through Licklider’s life. • Where Wizards Stay Up Late (Katie Hafner, Matthew Lyon) | 1960s to early 1970s The creation of ARPANET and the messy, human reality behind the internet’s birth. • Dealers of Lightning (Michael A. Hiltzik) | 1970s to 1980s Xerox PARC’s breakthroughs and the cautionary tale of inventing the future without capturing it. • The Soul of a New Machine (Tracy Kidder) | late 1970s to 1980 What it actually feels like to build hard technology under real pressure. • Fire in the Valley (Paul Freiberger, Michael Swaine) | 1970s to 1990s and beyond The personal computer revolution, told by the people who lived it. • A History of Modern Computing (Paul E. Ceruzzi) | late 1940s to 1990s A systems-level view that ties the entire evolution together. Links to all the books are in the comments. If you’ve read any of these or have others in the same vein, I’m always looking to expand this list.

  Big players eating big players. That’s pretty much the only way anyone is going to take on Stripe. Like it or not. The UK’s CMA just kicked off an investigation into Global Payments’ plan to buy Worldpay. It is a pretty massive move. If it goes through, the combined company would: 👉 Process close to 94 billion transactions a year 👉 Cover 6 million clients 👉 Operate across 175+ countries That’s huge. And it shows why this deal matters, you need that kind of scale if you’re even trying to stand in Stripe’s shadow as they seem to be winning more enterprise merchants... by the day. # Stripe's Private Status: Why the Delay

This title was summarized by AI from the post below.

[Zennon Kapron](https://www.linkedin.com/in/zennon?trk=public_post_feed-actor-name)  Zennon Kapron is an Influencer

* [Report this post](/uas/login?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Fposts%2Fzennon_why-stripe-wont-commit-to-an-ipo-activity-7421564457606270976-Fy_R&trk=public_post_ellipsis-menu-semaphore-sign-in-redirect&guestReportContentType=POST&_f=guest-reporting)

[Stripe](https://www.linkedin.com/company/stripe?trk=public_post-text) is one of the oldest fintech unicorns to remain a private company. Founded in 2010, Stripe is arguably past prime time to go public. Why the delay? It’s complicated. With a valuation of $106.7 billion, the San Francisco and Dublin-headquartered company is one of the most successful payment startups of all time. Its seed round backers included Sequoia, Elon Musk and Peter Thiel – who all have records of making extraordinarily successful bets on nascent upstarts. The company generates US$5.84 billion in revenue annually and serves millions of businesses. It has expanded beyond payments to become a full-stack financial infrastructure platform. It has added services like subscription management, business setup, fraud prevention, lending and revenue/tax automation. Unsurprisingly, Stripe is leaning into its AI capabilities as it seeks to capitalize on the massive expectations that investors and large corporations have for the technology. While some startups would seek to use the momentum from AI-fueled growth to pave the way for an IPO, Stripe has shown no such inclination. Co-founders Patrick and John Collison have said that public companies are often suited for the “extract stage” rather than the “expand stage.” They say that staying private allows the company to focus on infrastructure building and long-term investments without the constant scrutiny and pressure to meet quarterly earnings per share (EPS) targets that come with being publicly traded. Still, there are drawbacks to Stripe’s approach. On the one hand, tender offers and share buybacks may provide some liquidity to employees, this is a temporary fix and not a sustainable, long-term alternative to public market access. Secondly, kicking the can down the road indefinitely could result in a lower valuation when the company does eventually go public. Stripe may be the highest-flying payments startup today, but that may not be the case in three or five years.   Most startups rush to add a paywall. Notion refused to. They launched in 2016. By 2019, they hit 1M users.  By 2021, they were at 20M users and raised $275M at a $10B valuation. That’s the part SaaS founders choose to ignore: They didn’t monetize urgency. They monetized trust at scale. Open Notion for the first time and notice what doesn’t happen: No credit card wall No “upgrade now” pressure No artificial limits screaming at you No onboarding. You just start building. You’re not pushed to pay. You’re allowed to build. That wasn’t generosity. That was product strategy. Notion’s bet was simple: If people feel safe, they’ll stay. If they stay, paying becomes obvious later. And when monetization did show up, it was clean: Plus starts around $8/user/month annually (higher monthly). By then, teams weren’t thinking “Should we pay?” They were thinking: “We already rely on this. Let’s make it official.” What do you think? Paywall or not?   Only 5 things matter if you want to win in business. Well actually you don’t need all 5, but you can’t win with zero. I’ve spent time studying companies that actually won markets (Uber, Bolt, Amazon, Stripe), and building ventures myself. The patterns are boring. The outcomes are not. Here’s some truths you can internalize: 1. Distribution beats product. Every time. Whoever has the most reliable access to the customer wins more customers, even with an inferior product. Uber didn’t win because ridesharing was new. They won because they owned the moment you needed to move. Access > ideas. 2. Capital is a weapon, not a badge. Ever played poker against a big chip stack? They don’t need better cards. They can just bleed you out. Same in startups. Capital buys you: -Time -Mistakes -Market patience This is why “great companies die” and average ones survive. 3. Reach compounds faster than execution. The best story, told clearly, to the most people, over time wins. Not hype, Clarity. If people remember you, you’re already ahead. Distribution of belief matters as much as distribution of product. 4. Unfair protection is real (and underrated). Patents. Regulation. Data. Network position. Switching costs. Sometimes it’s tech. Sometimes it’s trust. Sometimes it’s just being embedded so deeply that replacing you feels painful. Every enduring business has a reason it shouldn’t be copied easily. Find yours. 5. Network effects end the game. When every new user makes the product better for the next user, the market tilts permanently. Think of it as a hive mind that evolves. This is when growth stops being linear and starts being inevitable. But here’s the uncomfortable part: Most startups never reach this stage. They die before the flywheel spins. The mistake founders make? Trying to win on everything. The truth: You only need one strong angle, but you must own it completely! Uber owned availability. Amazon owned selection. Stripe owned developer trust. Everything else is noise. Forget vanity metrics. Forget copying competitors blindly. Find your angle. Protect it. Compound it. That’s how markets are actually won. Depending on your lens, this is either a “down-round exit” or one of the most strategic moves we’ve seen from a major bank in business payments. Here’s what stands out to me: - This isn’t just a card portfolio deal. Capital One is effectively buying an AI‑native spend management operating system: corporate cards, expense automation, bill pay, and real‑time policy enforcement in one stack. - Brex proved that modern finance teams want software first, cards and accounts second. Capital One is admitting that the future of commercial banking is distribution + balance sheet wrapped around a software layer, not the other way around. - Brex is exiting at a steep discount to its peak valuation, but into a platform that can put its tech in front of millions of businesses and a massive balance sheet. For founders, that’s a reminder: strategic fit can matter more than private‑market markups. Bigger picture, this deal accelerates three trends: 1. Consolidation: The “standalone” spend‑management category just lost one of its biggest independent players, which raises the stakes for the rest of the ecosystem (Ramp, traditional issuers, and vertical SaaS finance tools). 2. AI in the core stack: This is a bet that AI‑driven policy enforcement, real‑time analytics, and automated reconciliation will be embedded into the core banking experience, not sold as a point solution. 3. Bank–fintech convergence: [Capital One](https://www.linkedin.com/company/capital-one?trk=public_post-text) now pairs a national franchise and payments network with a cloud‑native, global spend platform that already has EU licensing and enterprise‑grade capabilities.   Building a startup can feel like working in a vacuum. You wake up every day convinced there is something real here, but the outside world is quiet. No applause. No signals. Just you, your team, and a problem you cannot let go of. You pitch. You refine. You wait. Sometimes it feels like shouting into space and listening to your own echo. Every founder building what later becomes a unicorn passes through this phase. Before Stripe, there were years of quiet payments infrastructure work no one talked about. Before Flutterwave became a reference point, it was just a small team trying to make cross-border payments work when most people did not think it mattered. The vacuum is not a sign you are failing. It is often a sign you are early. Most meaningful companies are built while the world is distracted elsewhere. Progress looks invisible before it looks obvious. The loneliness you feel is not isolation. It is focus without validation. If you are still showing up, still learning, still improving the product when no one is watching, you are doing the hard part most people never see. That quiet work is what eventually bends attention in your direction. The vacuum does not mean you are unseen forever. It just means the signal is still forming. If you’ll be there and want to talk about your payment opportunities in 2026, contact Gareth to set up a meeting. #ICEBarcelona #ICE26 #Barcelona #GamingIndustry #payments #BlackStripe [Likes: 5, Comments: 0]; **Black Stripe** (5mo): As we head to the end of a successful year, we have agreed that our word-of-the-year was most definitely STABLECOINS. To find out more about stablecoins, read our quick-fire Q&A with Black Stripe founder Gareth Twist. Q: What do business leaders need to know in 2025? Stablecoins create efficiencies! And everyone wants efficiencies. Q: What exactly are stablecoins? Digital assets that are designed to maintain stable value and are pegged to a fiat currency. Q: Why are businesses suddenly paying attention to them? Business leaders are attracted because they offer price stability, instant global fund transfers, and settlement. They offer near-instant, programmable transfers 24/7, worldwide. Ideal for crossborder payments as they don't depend on traditional banking clearing systems. Q: Which stablecoins are most relevant? • USDT (Tether) • USDC (Circle) Q: How can businesses start exploring stablecoins safely? 1. Choose a specific use and try using stablecoins for that first, such as vendor payouts. 2. Work with a partner that provides full KYC/KYB, AML, and on- and off-ramp compliance. 3. Test-run a small part of the business with trusted partners. 4. Integrate gradually into your payment operations, and then you can evaluate the cost, speed and other important metrics for your business. Q: How does this connect to traditional payment flows? Major banking networks such as Visa and Mastercard are now supporting stablecoin settlements; they are using integrated stablecoin rails without changing the customer-facing process. It's going on successfully behind the scenes. Stablecoins connect first and last mile FX payments in fiat. They remove the clunky, costly and slow traditional payment rails and enable efficient and instant global money transfers. Q: How can Black Stripe help? Our clients who are exploring stablecoins often need more than just that; they also need infrastructure. Through txn.io , we can provide payments connectivity that supports both traditional and digital rails. Happy holidays and here's to a smooth and successful 2026. With a long-standing history in the superyacht industry and the power of technology at our fingertips to connect people oceans apart, Gareth Twist, CEO of Black Stripe , spoke with Captain Dan Ross of the S/Y Bundalong to explore a trend that’s gaining real momentum: crypto payments at sea. Captain Dan runs a tight ship, with a global itinerary, and, like himself, a young, digitally savvy crew. And like many in the industry, he's starting to see crypto not as a novelty, but as a necessary evolution. Here’s what he shared: Q: Captain Dan, is there really a place for crypto in yachting? A: “Absolutely. Especially with APA payments. Crypto enables us to move quickly, eliminating the need to wait on banks or expose card information. The reality is that most crew are already using it personally. They’re open to it. This isn’t the future, it’s now.” Q: What’s broken with current payment systems? A: “We constantly email credit card details for provisioning. One of ours has a US$50,000 limit — imagine what would happen if that fell into the wrong hands. And we’re not a big boat by industry standards. Salaries can be delayed due to differences in time zones, SWIFT network delays, or compliance requirements. It’s a headache for us and the crew.” Q: How does crypto actually improve things? A: There are four key areas where crypto is particularly successful: Speed: Instant payments to crew or suppliers, anywhere in the world. Security: No reused credentials, every transaction is a secure, isolated transfer. Cost: Avoids high foreign exchange fees and banking charges when transferring money internationally. Transparency: On-chain records add an extra layer of clarity — no lost wires or disputes. Q: Are platforms ready to support this? A: “Yes, companies like txn.pro are building regulated solutions designed for high-risk, high-mobility sectors like ours. They operate under licences in Lithuania, Canada, and Georgia, so you’re not flying blind when it comes to compliance.” Q: What’s the outlook for crypto and yachts over the next few years? A: “I see crew salaries going crypto, especially stablecoins. I see APA wallets being crypto-native. I see less dependence on banks that don’t understand our world. We’ll still need education and regulatory alignment, but the ball is already rolling.” Some of the recent superyacht trends have been: •⁠ ⁠Camper & Nicholsons began accepting crypto in 2022 •⁠ ⁠A Greenline 45 Coupe was fully sold using Bitcoin in 2025 •⁠ ⁠According to a Dockwalk crew survey in 2024, 60% of crew under 35 already hold crypto assets.
